newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 13.

text.p: Following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Thursday:
- An estimated six million Irish pounds is to be spend on implementing new tighter measures for the manufacture of meat and bone meal, Agriculture Minister Ivan Yates said on Wednesday.
- The Irish government on Wednesday night agreed to a powerful new Commission on Nursing in the hope it will head off the threatened strike by nurses.
- A new deal to encourage another 750 personnel to retire early from the Defence Forces was offered by the Irish government to all ranks on Wednesday.
- The Irish government on Wednesday night helped clear the way for the controversial deal under which Esat Digifone hopes to place its mobile phone antennae on police stations masts.
- The introduction of the 48-hour week could be phased in over two years thanks to a last-minute amendment tabled on Wednesday by Labour Affairs Minister Eithne Fitzgerald.

- Fears of an escalation of IRA violence and a backlash by loyalist paramilitaries have been intensified by the shooting dead of a British soldier manning a checkpoint at Beesbrook, County Armagh, Northern Ireland.
- The 30 percent pay claim by Ireland's members of parliament has been rejected by the Review Body on Higher Remuneration in the Public Sector.

- Documents and computer print-outs containing the names, addresses and accounts numbers of Ulster Bank customers were scattered around Dublin city centre after they were mistaken for ordinary rubbish.
- The Irish Prime Minister John Bruton made another strong attack on the IRA within hours of the shooting of a soldier in Armagh.

- The Italian Prime Minister, Romano Prodi on Wednesday claimed that Italy has adopted the toughest and most appropriate measures to ensure that the Italian economy meets the Maastricht convergence criteria for EMU.
- Two government ministers are drawing up plans to counteract a serious shortage of graduates that threatens job creation.
- The Stormont all-party talks on Northern Ireland are on the verge of collapse because Unionist and SDLP delegates have been unable to bridge the gap on arms decommissioning.

- Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke and the Bank of England governor Eddie George clashed publicly over monetary policy on Wednesday with the central bank insisting interest rates needed to rise while Clarke again rejected its advice.
- Ireland may be heading into another currency crisis similar to that of 1992/93 but cutting interest rates is not the solution, a top economist warned on Wednesday night.
